video_title: Consumers Feel Awful But Keep Spending with Michelle Meyer, Mastercard's Chief Economist
gist: Mastercard chief economist Michelle Meyer argues the US consumer remains supported by a balanced labor market (openings-to-unemployed just above 1) and wealth effects, forecasting 5.5% holiday spend growth ex-autos/gas (about half real volume) despite weak sentiment. She flags energy/diesel as the threat to real wages and shares Mastercard data showing AI-subscription users shop across more merchants and start holiday shopping earlier.

themes.theme: Holiday spend forecast & nominal vs real

insights.claim: Mastercard forecasts 5.5% year-over-year growth in US holiday retail spending (ex-autos and gas) for 2026, the strongest in four years.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Supports bullish positioning in retailers into Q4; consensus fears of a consumer slowdown may be overdone.
insights.quote: we're looking for 5.5% year-over-year growth in holiday spend this year. That's the strongest in four years.

insights.claim: Mastercard estimates roughly half of the holiday retail spending gain is inflation and half is real volume growth, which Meyer calls a healthy breakdown.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Implies ~2.5-3% real holiday volume growth; pricing power is contributing but not the whole story.
insights.quote: we estimate about half of the gain in retail spend is due to inflation, but that means the other half is due to real volumes.

insights.claim: Gasoline spending is running roughly 15-20% higher year over year because of higher pump prices, which is why Mastercard excludes autos and gas from its holiday measure.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Energy price spike is a live headwind for discretionary wallets and a tailwind for fuel retailers/energy.
insights.quote: People are spending nearly, you know, 15 20% year-over-year gains in at at the pump because of higher prices.

insights.claim: Meyer recommends splitting spending into number of transactions versus average transaction value to separate real volume from pricing effects, alongside Mastercard's high-frequency SpendingPulse metric segmented by merchant category (MCC).
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: A practical lens for reading retailer comps and Mastercard data: ticket growth vs traffic growth.
insights.quote: break down spending between the number of transactions versus the average transaction value

themes.theme: Labor market as primary consumer driver

insights.claim: Meyer argues the labor market, not interest rates, is the primary driver of US consumer spending, with unemployment hovering just above 4%, faster churn, and broadening job creation.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Watch payrolls/claims over rate moves to call consumer turns.
insights.quote: the primary driver for consumer spending is the labor market.

insights.claim: Construction job growth is being driven not by residential housing but by infrastructure buildout supporting AI capex, and manufacturing is also adding jobs with ISM surveys in expansion.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: AI capex is spilling into blue-collar employment, broadening the AI trade into industrials/construction.
insights.quote: You have construction jobs that are picking up, not because of residential, but because of all the infrastructure that's being built in the economy to support the capex, the AI investment.

insights.claim: The ratio of job openings to unemployed workers is now just above one, versus nearly 2-to-1 in 2022-2023, which Meyer describes as an optimal equilibrium.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Labor market in balance reduces both recession and wage-price-spiral tail risks.

insights.claim: Meyer's framework: if job switchers' wage growth begins outpacing job stayers', the labor market is too hot and the Fed may need to hike; if openings dry up relative to job seekers, it signals corporate retrenchment.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Switcher-vs-stayer wage gap is a leading indicator for Fed hiking risk.
insights.quote: job switchers start to outpace the wage growth of job stayers. And that shows a labor market that's probably too hot

insights.claim: Meyer flags two labor indicators beyond headlines: breadth (diffusion) of job creation across sectors and labor turnover/re-employment likelihood; both currently look supportive.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Defines what to monitor for an early labor-driven consumer crack.

themes.theme: Rates, wealth effects and the K-shape

insights.claim: With the 30-year fixed mortgage above 7%, higher rates hurt new buyers and ARM holders, but households locked into 2.5-3% COVID-era mortgages benefit from strong equity markets and higher yields on cash.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Rate hikes transmit weakly to the consumer aggregate; housing is the pinch point, not spending broadly.
insights.quote: with a 30-year fixed rate mortgage now above 7% it's getting you know that much more expensive

insights.claim: Upper-income households benefit disproportionately from balance-sheet wealth effects and are growing spending faster, but spending is still increasing across all income groups rather than contracting for lower-income households.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the 'low-end consumer collapse' narrative; low-end retailers may be less at risk than feared.
insights.quote: it is not the case that spending is contracting for the lower income.

insights.claim: Consumer spending is heavily supported by asset-price-driven net worth gains, implying spending, especially at the high end, is exposed to an equity market drawdown.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Second-order: a stock-market correction could hit the very cohort carrying spending growth.

insights.claim: Consumer sentiment surveys such as University of Michigan tracked spending until right after the pandemic; the gap opened in 2022 on inflation and never closed even as inflation moderated.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Don't trade sentiment surveys as a spending signal; hard data diverges persistently.
insights.quote: even once inflation over the next few years started to come back in back closer to core, the gap never really resolved itself.

insights.claim: Meyer cautions that falling survey response rates and sample representativeness issues mean sentiment surveys should be taken with a grain of salt.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Methodology issues weaken bearish narratives built on survey data.

insights.claim: Meyer argues the cumulative price level looks acceptable when measured relative to wages and asset prices, both of which have also inflated, so CPI and core PCE look reasonable in context.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Economist view that the 'affordability crisis' framing overstates real damage for the aggregate household.

insights.claim: Wages are currently running very close to headline inflation, so a continued rise in energy prices could tip the US into negative real wage growth; persistence is what matters.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Real wages are on a knife edge; energy prices are the swing factor for consumer health.
insights.quote: right now wages are hovering very close to headline inflation.

insights.claim: Meyer warns rising diesel prices could pass through into underlying goods inflation if input costs become too high for retailers and wholesalers.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Diesel is a leading indicator for core goods inflation and retail margin pressure.
insights.quote: pay close attention to diesel prices as well particularly because there's a threat that diesel prices could pass into underlying goods inflation

insights.claim: Mastercard data shows consumers with AI subscriptions ('AI power users') spread spending across a wider number of merchants, especially in beauty services, specialty food stores, restaurants and florists.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: AI-driven discovery erodes incumbent merchant concentration in search-heavy categories and favors niche/small merchants.
insights.quote: AI power users go to a wider number of merchants to spend.

insights.claim: AI users show no greater merchant dispersion than non-AI users in video game stores, home improvement or grocery stores.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Big-box category leaders (grocery, home improvement) appear insulated from AI-driven share dispersion for now.

insights.claim: AI users engage earlier in the holiday shopping season, while non-AI users concentrate more spending at the very end of the season.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: AI adoption may pull holiday demand forward, distorting weekly/monthly holiday read-throughs.
insights.quote: there's an earlier engagement in the holiday season for AI users

insights.claim: Meyer says consumers have more power because of information access, making them value-optimizers who can source alternatives including overseas, lowering barriers to entry for small businesses and increasing retail innovation.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Pricing power for undifferentiated retailers is structurally pressured.
insights.quote: the barriers to entry for small businesses are lower.

insights.claim: Mastercard sees the global economy continuing to expand into 2027, particularly the US, with the key question being how much more investment, especially AI adoption-related capex, will drive growth.
insights.speaker: Michelle Meyer
insights.so_what: Growth outlook hinges on continuation of the AI capex cycle; a capex pause is the key macro risk.
insights.quote: a big question I think for 27 is how much more investment will we see across the globe particularly related to the adoption of AI.
